# @sanity/workflow-blueprint

## 0.36.0

### Minor Changes

- 90d0053: `@sanity/workflow-blueprint` now exports `describeWorkflowsResource` to produce labeled, JSON-safe display details for a planned Workflows resource and optional deployed definition results. The restricted provider records those details in `providerMetadata.workflowDisplay` after a successful create or update, alongside the existing `deployId` and `results`. This metadata is a snapshot of that operation; existing or attached resources may lack it. The Blueprints CLI does not yet display these details.

  **No upgrade action required.** Consumers that want to render Workflows details can call the helper with a `defineWorkflows` resource and pass deployed definitions only when they have actual results.

  **Docs impact:** Add the display helper, its descriptor rows, and last-successful-operation metadata semantics to the Workflows Blueprint API reference and resource guide. Keep local-plan and remote-info display guidance pending until the external CLI consumes the descriptor.

- 12240b6: The generated start watcher for a `types`-less subject entry now carries a type leg excluding the engine's own documents, `!(_type in [...])`, instead of no type leg at all. A watcher is a prefilter, so it still fires on the rest of the reserved `sanity.` and `system.` namespaces and the runtime declines those.

  Run `sanity-workflows blueprint generate` after upgrading and redeploy the blueprint: without it the deployed watcher keeps firing on every create in the dataset, including the instance each start creates.

  **Docs impact:** Update the Blueprints generation guide where it describes the type-less watcher's filter.

- 9902088: **BREAKING:** An effect's `runtime` function budget is validated against the range Sanity Functions accepts, so a definition the platform would reject at `blueprints deploy` now fails at `defineWorkflow`. The old contract accepted any positive integer for `timeout` and `memory`, and documented `memory` in megabytes. The new contract takes `timeout` as a whole number of seconds from 1 to 900 and `memory` as a whole number of gigabytes from 1 to 10. Anything else (zero, a fraction, or a value over the limit) throws with the field, the unit, and the range named. This affects anyone whose definitions declare a budget, and in particular anyone who wrote `memory` in megabytes: `memory: 512` asks for 512 gigabytes and now fails at authoring. Without migrating, `defineWorkflow` throws and nothing in that module loads.

  Stored definitions are unaffected: nothing already deployed changes. To migrate, change a megabyte-shaped `memory` to the gigabytes you want (`512` becomes `1` unless the handler needs more) and bring any `timeout` over 900 down. A definition whose budget is already inside the range needs no change. The `@sanity/workflow-blueprint` generator emits the validated values unchanged, and its `FunctionLimits` type now documents `memory` in gigabytes.

  **Docs impact:** Update the `runtime` block section of the `@sanity/workflow-blueprint` README and the runtime reference to state both units with their accepted ranges and that an out-of-range budget fails at `defineWorkflow`; the release notes should name the megabyte-to-gigabyte correction so a reader who wrote `512` knows why authoring now rejects it.

- 0e072b9: `sanity-workflows deploy` now checks the generated Blueprints runtime against the definitions it is about to deploy. After the definitions validate, the deploy looks for `workflows.blueprint.ts` next to `sanity.workflow.ts`. When that file is there, the deploy runs the same comparison as `blueprint generate --check`: a regenerated shell that differs from disk, or a declared effect with no handler, exits non-zero before the first definition reaches the dataset and before a token is resolved, naming each file and the command that fixes it. When no generated runtime is there, the deploy prints the runtime the definitions need and continues; definitions needing no functions print nothing, and definitions no runtime can be derived from print a warning. `deploy --check` and `deploy --dry-run` run the check too, so `deploy --check` is a complete offline pre-flight. The deploy never writes a source file, because generation stays the explicit `blueprint generate` command.

  Teams with no generated runtime need **no upgrade action**: nothing is compared and the deploy behaves as before, apart from a report of what a generated runtime would contain. Teams that do generate one must keep it current, because a deploy now stops on drift instead of shipping definitions their runtime cannot serve: run `sanity-workflows blueprint generate`, review the result, and deploy again. The check covers the whole config, since the generated tree declares every deployment in it, so a targeted `deploy --deployment one` also stops when a sibling deployment has drifted or its definitions no longer validate. There is no flag or configuration key that turns the check off; a project that hand-writes its runtime has no generated tree for the check to compare.

  `@sanity/workflow-blueprint` exports `generatedRuntimeAlignment` from `@sanity/workflow-blueprint/generate` for callers that need that verdict themselves. It takes the directory holding the config file, reads only that directory, writes nothing, and returns the runtime the definitions need, the tree they would generate, and every planned file that differs from disk. It also takes an optional `compiler`, the TypeScript 6 compiler API used to wire an existing `sanity.blueprint.ts`; pass it when the host project's installed `typescript` package is absent or is TypeScript 7, which does not expose that API, and omit it to use the installed package. The generated resources module's own path is exported alongside it as `WORKFLOW_RESOURCES_PATH`.

  **No upgrade action required** for existing callers of `generatedRuntimeAlignment`: `compiler` is optional and omitting it preserves the prior behavior.

  **Docs impact:** Update the CLI reference for `deploy`, `deploy --check`, and `deploy --dry-run` to state that the alignment check runs by default and cannot be turned off, the generated-runtime guide to describe deploy-time drift as the second gate beside the CI `blueprint generate --check` job, including the whole-config scope of a targeted deploy, and the `@sanity/workflow-blueprint` API reference for `generatedRuntimeAlignment` to document its optional `compiler` parameter.

- 12240b6: **BREAKING:** The generated blueprint's trigger filters are now compiled per function, and the emitted heartbeat is scoped to the workflows it is responsible for. Anyone calling the helpers below or reading `drainFilter` directly must update the call. A generated tree still on disk must be regenerated, or its functions keep firing on writes that cannot change a workflow.
  - `DeploymentEmission.drainFilter` is gone: each `DrainSpec` carries its own `filter`, naming only the effects that drain runs.
  - `drainEffectsFilter(tag)` now takes `{tag, effectNames}`.
  - `startWatcherFilter(subjectTypes)` now takes `{subjectTypes, updates}`.
  - `startWatcherName(tag, dataset)` now takes `{tag, dataset, group}`, with `group` required.
  - `RuntimeNeeds` drops `drain.needed`, `heartbeat.needed` and `startWatch.needed`. Read the sibling arrays instead: `effectNames.length > 0`, `timeSites.length > 0 || spawnSites.length > 0`, and `deployment.definitions.some(startableFromAWrite)`, which `@sanity/workflow-blueprint/generate` exports. The sibling `startWatch.definitions` holds names, and it lists every autonomous definition, including ones no write can start.
  - `heartbeatShellModule`'s `heartbeat` carries the new required `HeartbeatSpec.definitions`, and `StartWatcherSpec` carries the new required `updates`.
  - `sweepAndTickInFlight` is now `runHeartbeat`, taking a required `definitions` and an optional `catchUp` with a required `recoverDefinitions`. `SweepAndTickResult` is now `HeartbeatResult`, which gains `caughtUp`, `caughtUpUnsettled` and `deferred`.

  `@sanity/workflow-blueprint/generate` adds `watchedUpdatesOf` with its `WatchedUpdates` result, `assertEmittablePath`, `RuntimeNeeds.heartbeat.spawnSites` with its `DefinitionSpawnSite` entries, and `HeartbeatSpec.catchUp` typed as the new `HeartbeatCatchUpSpec`. `@sanity/workflow-blueprint/runtime` adds `beatCatchUp` with its `BeatCatchUp` result, `HeartbeatCatchUpArgs`, and `HEARTBEAT_BEAT_MS`, the period the generated beat uses.

  What changes at run time: a drain fires only on an instance write that touched `pendingEffects` and left one of its own effects unclaimed, so a comment or assignee change invokes nothing, and an effect hosted on a durable function or self-hosted is not a reason to invoke it. Start watchers are emitted per definition, not one per dataset: a definition whose filter accepts updates gets `wf-<tag>-start-<dataset>-<definition>` carrying only the paths it reads, and the definitions that watch creates alone share `wf-<tag>-start-<dataset>-creates`. A deployment with only creates-only definitions therefore sees its single watcher renamed, which regenerating carries. A leftover `functions/wf-*-start-*` directory from the old name is inert, because the blueprint lists each function by its `src`; regenerating is sufficient. A start watcher fires on a create, or on an update that changed a field an autonomous definition's `start.filter` reads; a filter that reads none of the written document's own fields but `_type`, which no write can change, watches creates only, and one whose truth can change without a write to the subject keeps every update and is reported in the new `DeploymentPlan.unnarrowedStartFilters`, which covers a filter reading the document in a way no field path describes, one reading another document through a scan or a dereference, and one reading `$now`. A document that becomes eligible by time alone still starts on its next write, because applicability is evaluated on a write. A definition reading nothing of the subject, the dataset or the clock starts each document once, at its creation: one that existed before its watcher deployed starts only when you start it explicitly, or once the definition gains a start filter reading the subject or the dataset. A heartbeat is emitted when a `'function'`-hosted workflow reads `$now` or spawns children, and whenever the deployment declares a `'function'`-hosted effect at all; it ticks only the `'function'`-hosted workflows it names in `heartbeat.definitions`, which is empty when it exists solely to recover queues, and recovers the queues of the workflows in `heartbeat.catchUp.recoverDefinitions` whatever kind hosts them. Spawning is a new heartbeat reason, so a parent whose gates read `$subworkflows` is re-evaluated after a child settles instead of stalling until someone opens it. Each beat also drains the instances holding an effect no drainer is working on, whether unclaimed for longer than one beat or left under a lapsed claim, including an instance that has already completed holding one, and reports what it settled and what it left unsettled in its log line, so deploying definitions before the functions, or a drain outage, loses no effect.

  The emitted heartbeat now also carries a budget: for each field some recoverable effect declares, the larger of the platform default and the largest declared value. Budgeted effects recover one per beat, and the beat dispatches its budgeted effect first: only the candidate query and that instance's claim sweep run before the handler, and ticks and unbudgeted recovery follow it, so a handler never executes in a budget smaller than its own declaration. `beatCatchUp` picks a beat's handlers and its `catchUp` argument together: it registers every unbudgeted effect plus one budgeted effect, taken in turn, and `runHeartbeat` drains a single instance holding that one. A budgeted effect's backlog clears one entry per beat whose turn it holds. `deferred` counts the instances whose budgeted dispatch a beat left to a later one; their unbudgeted entries are drained all the same. A beat spends its one budgeted run on an instance that held a claimable entry of that effect when the beat queried, so an entry whose claim lapses mid-beat is recovered by the next beat rather than this one. `runHeartbeat` and `beatCatchUp` throw on a `catchUp.afterMs` that is not a positive finite number.

  Run `sanity-workflows blueprint generate` after upgrading and redeploy the blueprint; the emitted filters, the heartbeat shell, the heartbeat's budget and which deployments emit a heartbeat at all change. A hand-written beat must move to `beatCatchUp` for its handler registry and pass the new `catchUp.recoverDefinitions`. The beat's operator log line and its all-failed error are respelled: the empty case reads `no instances to work on`, the summary `worked on N instances (…)` with the new counters, and the throw `every instance failed`. Repoint any alert or parser matching the old `ticked N in-flight instances` and `every tick failed`. Effect handlers, the handler registry and `sanity.workflow.ts` are untouched.

  **Docs impact:** Update the Blueprints generation guide and the runtime reference where they describe the drain and watcher triggers, the heartbeat's reasons, scope, budget and dispatch order, the `runtime` block's budget units, and `runHeartbeat`; document the deploy order (definitions first, then functions) now that the heartbeat's catch-up makes it lossless, and add the helper-signature migration to the release notes.

## 0.35.0

### Minor Changes

- a3489d2: Workflows CLI commands now load `sanity.workflow.ts` in projects using
  TypeScript 7. `blueprint generate` and `blueprint generate --check` work with
  TypeScript 6, TypeScript 7, or no project TypeScript installation: the CLI
  supplies its own TypeScript 6 compatibility compiler for editing an existing
  `sanity.blueprint.ts`. Direct generator callers can pass that API through
  `emissionWritePlan({compiler})` or as the second argument to `wireBlueprint`.
  When no usable compiler is available, direct wiring reports how to supply one.
  The Blueprint package root now exports `CONFIG_FILE_NAMES` so custom loaders
  can share the same config discovery order without importing the generator.
  The workflow engine and generated function runtimes do not acquire a compiler
  dependency.

  **No upgrade action required.** Install the updated Workflows release normally;
  keep your project's TypeScript version and existing config files.

  **Docs impact:** Update the Blueprint generation reference to explain the
  optional compiler argument and root `CONFIG_FILE_NAMES` export for direct
  callers, and the CLI installation guidance to say Blueprint commands work in
  projects using TypeScript 6, TypeScript 7, or no installed TypeScript.

## 0.34.0

### Minor Changes

- 00bb88f: **BREAKING:** `@sanity/workflow-blueprint` no longer exports `workflowProvider`, `ResolvedWorkflowResource`, `WorkflowResourceDefinitionSnapshot`, `WorkflowProvisionReceipt`, or the provision, read, rollback, and destroy provider functions and their supporting types. Blueprints backend integrations that import those APIs must install the restricted `@sanity/blueprints-resource-workflow` package and register its default provider export instead. Existing imports fail after upgrading until they migrate. Workflow authors can continue to use `defineWorkflows`, the manifest types, `/generate`, and `/runtime` from the public package.

  Public Blueprint authoring now accepts coordinator-owned `ownershipAction` values for attach and detach while preserving the existing `deletionPolicy: 'protect'` support. The public package also exports `parseWorkflowLifecycle` and `WorkflowsResourceOwnershipAction`. No upgrade action is required for workflow authors who do not use these lifecycle controls.

  The restricted provider uses the caller's token, consumes resolved same-Stack resource references, and compensates failed stack operations by deleting only the exact definition versions that operation created. Before the first automated release, a maintainer must bootstrap `@sanity/blueprints-resource-workflow`, configure this repository's `release.yml` workflow as its trusted publisher, and provide the repository's read-only npm configuration with access to install the restricted package.

  **Docs impact:** Update the Blueprint resource reference to keep only the public authoring and manifest APIs, add the restricted provider registration and first-publish procedure to release guidance, and preserve the existing generator and runtime guides.

## 0.33.0

### Minor Changes

- b3b2797: `@sanity/workflow-blueprint` gains two entry points beside the existing definer and provider.

  `@sanity/workflow-blueprint/generate` is the offline analysis of what a deployment's definitions require of a server-side runtime, and the plan for the functions that provide it. `runtimeNeeds(deployment)` performs no I/O: declared effects mean a drain must run their handlers, a condition reading `$now` means a clock must tick past the deadline, `start.kind: 'autonomous'` on a startable definition means a watcher must start instances from writes, and none of the above means no functions at all, because the reactive Studio session is already the runtime of a purely interactive workflow. `runtimeEmissionPlan(config)` turns those needs into the resources each deployment emits — the robot token, the drains, the scheduled heartbeat with the reasons it exists, and one start-watcher per dataset the deployment touches — and reports the autonomous definitions a needs report should warn about. The entry point also owns the emitted resource names and the compiled trigger filters. Roles, permission rules, and guards join it later.

  `@sanity/workflow-blueprint/runtime` is the wiring a generated function shell imports. `createRuntimeEngine(deployment, {context})` turns a Sanity Function context into a scoped engine and the client it runs on, with a raw-perspective client pinned to the engine's API version, cross-resource routing derived from `resourceAliases`, and a `server` execution identity named after the deployment's robot token. `sweepAndTickInFlight` is the heartbeat loop: it ticks every in-flight instance in the tag, releases effect claims whose lease lapsed, isolates one instance's failure, and throws when every candidate failed so the invocation reports red instead of a green no-op.

  **No upgrade action required.** The `.` entry point is unchanged, so existing `defineWorkflows` and `workflowProvider` users are unaffected. Both new entry points plan and wire; neither writes files, so adopting `generate` today means reading the needs analysis rather than deploying generated functions.

  **Docs impact:** Add a Workflows runtime concept page covering the four needs and the zero-functions answer, and extend the Blueprints guide with the two new entry points and the `runtime` block. The engine's `createEngine` reference should point at `createRuntimeEngine` as the supported way to build an engine inside a Sanity Function.

- b3b2797: Where the generated unattended runtime hosts a workflow or an effect is declared as one `runtime` block on three authoring nodes: the deployment in `sanity.workflow.ts`, the workflow in `defineWorkflow`, and the effect node. `kind` is `'function'` (a plain Sanity Function), `'durableFunction'` (a durable one), or `'selfHosted'` (a process you run yourself). Each level inherits from the one above, so a workflow that declares no block takes its deployment's kind and an effect takes its workflow's. Omit it everywhere and everything hosts on `'function'`. `kind` is the whole block at the deployment and workflow levels; an effect's `'function'` block also carries the function budget, `timeout` in seconds and `memory` in megabytes, and an effect that declares either gets its own drain function so an expensive handler's budget does not size every other handler's. An unknown kind fails at `defineWorkflow` or `defineWorkflowConfig`, before any deploy runs, naming the three accepted members; a budget on any other kind is rejected there too.

  `@sanity/workflow-blueprint`'s emission plan groups by resolved kind. A `'function'` workflow gets the drain, the heartbeat, and the start watcher it always got. A `'durableFunction'` workflow or effect is listed under `planned.hosting` and emits nothing yet, while the rest of the deployment emits normally, with no error and no whole-deployment refusal. A `'selfHosted'` workflow or effect emits nothing, is skipped by the generated drains, is left out of the generated handler registry, and is reported under `planned.selfHosted`, which names the deadlines that process must tick, the effects it must drain, the parents it must re-evaluate when a child settles, and the autonomous definitions it must start. Two definitions in one deployment that host the same effect name differently fail generation, because one effect name has one handler and one budget. A start watcher is emitted for a durable workflow as well as a function-hosted one, because starting an instance does not depend on the host.

  The block is authoring-only. `defineWorkflow` returns the stored definition plus the `runtime` the generator reads, and the deploy strips it: it never reaches the Content Lake, the stored definition schema rejects it, and two definitions that differ only in a hosting kind fingerprint identically, so changing a kind never mints a definition version. It does change the emitted tree, so regenerate afterwards and delete the function directories the new tree no longer contains.

  **No upgrade action required.** Nothing this release replaces has been published: the deployment `runtime` block and the `@sanity/workflow-blueprint/generate` entry point that exposed the earlier planning helpers both ship for the first time here. Declare a block only where you want to move a workflow or an effect off the default.

  **Docs impact:** Document the `runtime` block once, at all three levels, in the deployment configuration reference beside `tag`, `workflowResource`, and `resourceAliases`: each kind, what the generator emits for it, and the effect-level `timeout` and `memory` units. Add the four hosting shapes (function hosted, durable hosted, self hosted with one workflow kept on functions, and mixed inside one workflow) to the generated-runtime guide, and state there that hosting decides whether a `$now` deadline causes a heartbeat to be emitted rather than which instances an emitted heartbeat ticks. State in the data-model concepts that `runtime` is the authoring-only block tooling reads and the deploy never stores.

- b7510cc: **BREAKING:** `runtimeEmissionPlan` now rejects a config whose deployments emit colliding resource names. Two deployments sharing a tag collide when both emit runtime resources; a deployment with no runtime emission may share a tag. Callers with colliding resources receive a `ContractViolationError` naming both deployments. Give those deployments distinct tags and verify that their emitted names are unique before upgrading; until the collisions are resolved, planning throws instead of returning an invalid blueprint.

  `@sanity/workflow-blueprint/generate` now renders the whole runtime file tree, not just the plan behind it. `emissionWritePlan` turns a `runtimeEmissionPlan` into every file body a deployment's definitions require: `workflows.blueprint.ts` exporting `workflowResources` (the `defineWorkflows` entry per deployment, the runtime robot token, and one `defineDocumentFunction` or `defineScheduledFunction` per emitted function), one `functions/<name>/index.ts` shell and `package.json` per function, `effect-handlers/all.ts` typing `effectHandlers` as `Record<DeclaredEffectName, EffectHandler>`, and one scaffold-once handler stub per declared effect name. Each planned file carries an ownership tag that decides whether a writer may replace what is on disk: `generated` shells are rewritten every run, `scaffold` stubs are written only when absent so an implemented handler always survives, and the developer's own `sanity.blueprint.ts` receives the `workflowResources` import and one spread exactly once and is never rewritten after. Removing an effect from a definition drops its registry import and reports the now-orphaned handler file; removing the last effect reports the registry itself. The generator deletes nothing. Every template is a pure function over the plan and performs no I/O, so a host supplies what is on disk and applies the result.

  The `defineWorkflows` entry is emitted commented out, because the Blueprints service does not register the `sanity.workflow` resource type yet and one unknown resource fails the whole blueprint deploy, the emitted functions included. Keep deploying definitions with `npx @sanity/workflow-cli deploy`; the generated comment says so at the entry, and the import stays in place so uncommenting is the only edit once the provider is registered.

  Two further requirements apply to a config before it can be emitted. A deployment's `name` must be able to name a binding, because the generated modules import the deployment as a named export from `./sanity.workflow` under that name; rename a deployment such as `prod-eu` or `default`, and export it from the config module. A function shell imports it under the fixed local alias `deployment`, so a deployment named after something a shell itself binds needs no rename. A declared effect name must produce a distinct, usable handler binding: `all` (in any casing) is the registry's own module, `pay.out` and `pay-out` collapse to one identifier, two names differing only by case are one handler file on a case-insensitive filesystem, and a name whose identifier JavaScript will not accept as a binding, or that the registry module already binds (`effectHandlers`, `EffectHandler`, `DeclaredEffectName`), cannot be declared. Each of these fails emission with a message naming the offending values.

  Each generated function's `package.json` copies the specifications the project already declares for `@sanity/functions`, `@sanity/workflow-blueprint` and `@sanity/workflow-engine`, unchanged, so the functions and the project resolve against the same ranges. Emission fails naming any of the three the project declares nowhere, so install them before generating rather than shipping a guessed range.

  **No upgrade action required** for a config whose emitted resource names are already unique: the plan, needs analysis, definer and provider signatures are unchanged, and nothing writes files yet. The CLI command that applies this plan ships separately.

  Wiring the developer's `sanity.blueprint.ts` requires exactly one `resources` array literal among the object arguments of its `defineBlueprint(...)` calls. Other syntax receives a `manualBlueprintWiring` result with the import and spread to add. Comments, strings, template literals, regular expressions and resources arrays outside those calls are left alone. Wiring also requires a value import of `workflowResources` from `./workflows.blueprint` (with an optional `.ts` extension) and a `...workflowResources` spread. The generator inserts whichever is missing. Other bindings of `workflowResources`, including unrelated and type-only imports, require manual resolution before adding the generated import and spread.

  Because the generator parses TypeScript, `typescript` is declared as an **optional** peer dependency. Anything that imports `@sanity/workflow-blueprint/generate` must have TypeScript installed, which a project generating `.ts` files already does. It is optional so that deployed functions, which depend on this package for `@sanity/workflow-blueprint/runtime` alone, do not install a compiler they never load.

  A scaffold is never written over a file whose path differs from it only in case. Renaming an effect from `notify` to `Notify` plans `effect-handlers/Notify.ts` while `effect-handlers/notify.ts` holds the developer's implementation, and on a case-insensitive filesystem that write would replace it. `emissionWritePlan` matches planned paths against what is on disk without regard to case, writes neither path, and reports the pair through the new `caseCollisions` entry so the developer can rename the file and its exported handler. For `notify` to `Notify`, change the filename to `Notify.ts` and the exported binding to `Notify` to match the generated registry.

  The emitted tree is verified rather than only snapshotted: one test renders the whole tree, writes it to disk with a `sanity.workflow.ts`, and typechecks it with the TypeScript compiler against the packages it imports, requiring zero diagnostics; another imports the generated shells and drives each handler against the in-memory bench, asserting that the scaffolded stub fails the effect with its "not implemented" error, that an implemented handler completes it, that the heartbeat ticks an instance past its `$now` deadline, and that the start-watcher starts the autonomous definition for a watched subject type and nothing for any other.

  A staging probe app renders the same tree from the same library path and runs every generated function from a scratch consumer project built out of packed tarballs, against a real Sanity project: the start-watcher starts an instance for a written article, the drain runs the scaffolded stub and records its failure, and the heartbeat's tick releases the deadline and advances the stage. It records which steps the staging credentials cannot complete rather than passing silently.

  **Docs impact:** Document the two-zone generated tree and its ownership rules in the Workflows concepts material on deriving a runtime from definitions, alongside the existing needs-analysis coverage; the package README's new "The generated tree" section is the canonical description. Say plainly that definitions still deploy with `npx @sanity/workflow-cli deploy` while the `defineWorkflows` entry is commented out, matching the existing note about the unregistered resource type. The reference for `@sanity/workflow-blueprint/generate` needs the `emissionWritePlan` entry, the `PlannedWrite` ownership values, the `orphanedRegistry` and `caseCollisions` reports, the `wireBlueprint` entry and its `BlueprintWiring` result, and the naming rules for deployments and effect names. Note the optional `typescript` peer dependency wherever installing the package for generation is described. Hold the end-to-end walkthrough until the generate command lands, then point it at this tree.

- ba031fe: **BREAKING:** `emissionWritePlan` now requires `configFile`, the name of the config file the generated modules import their deployment from, and `readGenerationRoot` does not supply it — its return type is `Omit<EmissionWriteInputs, 'plan' | 'configFile'>`, because whoever loaded the config is the one who knows which accepted name it came from. The old input assumed `sanity.workflow.ts` and emitted an extensionless `./sanity.workflow` specifier for every config, so a project whose config is `sanity.workflow.mjs` got a tree whose every deployment import failed to resolve, with both `blueprint generate` and `--check` reporting success. Every caller of `emissionWritePlan` passes `configFile` — `emissionWritePlan({plan, configFile: 'sanity.workflow.ts', ...readGenerationRoot(root)})` reproduces the previous behaviour exactly. The emitted specifier is now extensionless for a `.ts` or `.js` config and the full file name for anything else, which is what TypeScript's bundler resolution finds. Not migrating leaves a `.mjs` project's generated tree unbuildable; a `.ts` project's output is byte-identical. `workflowResourcesModule` changes from a positional plan argument to `{plan, configModule}`, and `EmittedDeployment` — the object each shell template takes — gains a required `configModule`, so a caller rendering templates directly passes `configModuleSpecifier(configFile)` for both. `CONFIG_FILE_NAMES` is now exported from this entry point and is the list a loader should search.

  `@sanity/workflow-blueprint/generate` gains the filesystem half of the emission plan, so a generation step no longer hand-rolls its own reads and writes. `readGenerationRoot(root)` gathers the three inputs `emissionWritePlan` needs from a directory: the handler files already there, the developer's `sanity.blueprint.ts` source when it exists, and the dependency specifications the project's `package.json` declares. `applyEmissionWritePlan({root, plan})` writes the plan back into that directory and reports each file as `created`, `updated`, or `unchanged`; it throws before writing anything rather than replace a `scaffold` whose contents differ from the planned stub, so neither an incomplete `existingPaths` nor a plan kept across a handler edit can destroy an implemented handler — rebuild the plan whenever the root may have changed since it was read. `emissionDivergences({root, plan})` is the read-only half: every planned file that is `missing` or `differs`, and nothing at all when the tree on disk is the tree the plan would write. `DEVELOPER_BLUEPRINT_PATH` and `PROJECT_MANIFEST_PATH` name the two paths those functions read.

  `typecheckTree` in the private `@sanity/workflow-test-fixtures` gains an optional `allowJs`, needed to compile a tree that imports a JavaScript config.

  **Docs impact:** Update the Blueprints reference where it says the caller supplies what is on disk and applies the result, so it points at these functions and at `sanity-workflows blueprint generate` as the supported path. The cookbook chapter on running workflows on a server should route readers to the CLI command rather than to this API.

- ba031fe: A generated heartbeat is emitted as a plain `defineScheduledFunction` with no `project`. A deployed heartbeat in that shape is created by the platform and reported by `blueprints info`, and does not run.

  **Regenerate and redeploy if your definitions emit a heartbeat.** Run `npx @sanity/workflow-cli blueprint generate` and `npx sanity blueprints deploy`. Only `workflows.blueprint.ts` changes, the drain and start-watcher resources keep the `project` they legitimately carry, and no function directory is added or removed. A deployment with no `$now` deadline and no effect emits no heartbeat and is unaffected.

## 0.32.0

### Minor Changes

- bad8b1d: The Workflows Blueprint provider now returns each deployment target's deterministic external ID during pre-deploy without writing definitions. Blueprints hosts can reserve Stack ownership of that target and reject a competing Stack before its provider changes the Content Lake; the owning Stack's normal deploy then provisions through the existing update lifecycle.

  Blueprints API hosts must upgrade the provider, run pre-deploy before normal deploy, and reject ordinary create when the provider requires initialization; otherwise the ownership guarantee can be bypassed. **No upgrade action required** for direct Workflows engine or CLI consumers.

  **Docs impact:** Update the Blueprints deployment guide and lifecycle reference to explain the pre-deploy target-key handoff, Blueprints Stack ownership reservation, the two-phase deploy sequence, and the `(workflowResource, tag)` deployment-target boundary.

- 26dd4e5: Generated API references now include every type used by a public signature and link cross-package symbols to their authoritative package entry. Caller-facing helper contracts such as field mutation operations, engine operation context types, test-bench argument types, member avatar data, MCP client policy, and Studio user clients are now available as named exports where their public APIs already expose those shapes. GROQ condition consumers can import the documented `COMPARISON_OPS` list alongside its `ComparisonOp` type, while the shared cross-package exhaustiveness helper is an unsupported `@internal` export and is omitted from the reference.

  **No upgrade action required.** Existing imports and runtime behavior remain compatible; consumers may adopt the new named type exports instead of reconstructing those shapes locally.

  **Docs impact:** Refresh the generated API references for the affected packages; no conceptual guides, examples, or migration guidance need changes.

## 0.31.0

### Minor Changes

- f7bf46a: **BREAKING:** Editorial Workflows Blueprint resources now reject every `ownershipAction` and unknown lifecycle key at manifest evaluation and at the provider boundary. Integrations that supplied an ownership action or relied on an unknown lifecycle key being silently removed must remove it and use the default `retain` lifecycle (or `protect`); leaving it in place now fails validation instead of reaching a provider lifecycle path that cannot honor it.

  The package now exports the complete `defineWorkflows` resource definer and `workflowProvider` factory required to deploy Editorial Workflows definitions through Sanity Blueprints. Because Blueprints does not pass selected Stack context into `sanity.blueprint.ts`, the Editorial Workflows Blueprint convention requires `SANITY_WORKFLOW_TAG` to select exactly one tag group during module evaluation; `sanity blueprints deploy --stack <name-or-id>` independently selects the remote Stack that receives those generated `sanity.workflow` resources. The provider uses the deployment caller's token with public Sanity client APIs, derives a collision-safe external ID for each `(workflowResource, tag)` partition, reads the latest deployed state for manifest-managed definition names, and rolls back a successful create or update from its partition-bound deployment receipt.

  Rollback deletes only versions that operation created, in reverse dependency order and without cascading into instances; unchanged and earlier versions remain deployed, while absent versions and engine cleanup failures surface instead of reporting false success. Lifecycle normalization merges `deletionPolicy: 'retain'` when another supported lifecycle field is present, while raw `allow` and `replace` policies fail at the provider boundary. Provider setup rejects unknown Blueprints runtime environments, and ancillary logger failures do not change lifecycle action outcomes.

  This package release is a rollout prerequisite, not sufficient by itself to make `sanity blueprints deploy` accept Editorial Workflows resources. Upgrade this package first, then expose its `defineWorkflows` implementation from `@sanity/blueprints`, register its `workflowProvider` export in the Blueprints API, and complete the staging deployment checks before documenting the integration as available. No author action is required for resources that omit lifecycle configuration or already use `retain` or `protect` without an ownership action.

  **Docs impact:** Prepare a substantial Editorial Workflows Blueprints deployment guide and provider-reference update covering shared deployment objects, the required `SANITY_WORKFLOW_TAG` selector, selecting exactly one Workflows tag group in `sanity.blueprint.ts`, pairing that selection with the intended Blueprints Stack, retain removal versus stack-destruction behavior, unmanaged removed definitions, physical partition identity, deployment receipts, exact rollback, and unsupported ownership actions. Hold publication and availability claims until `@sanity/blueprints` exposes `defineWorkflows`, the Blueprints API registers `workflowProvider`, and the complete staging path passes.

## 0.30.0

### Minor Changes

- 90207dc: **BREAKING:** `assertReaderModelAcknowledgement` now requires `{requiredMinReaderModel, context?}` instead of a context string, and `ReaderModelAcknowledgementError` accepts its optional context through `{context}`. The Blueprint package's `AcknowledgedDeployment` type moves to the engine as `AcknowledgedWorkflowDeployment`; update imports and use that shared name. Assignment-valued fields can now declare a non-empty `roles` list that limits newly written assignees. Existing fields without `roles` stay unconstrained, retain reader floor 4, and continue deploying with `expectedMinReaderModel: 4`; installing this release requires no coordinated rollout or configuration change.

  Before adding `roles`, upgrade every Studio, CLI, MCP server, Function, and other runtime that shares the affected workflow resource, then change that deployment's literal `expectedMinReaderModel` to `8`. MCP deployments pass the same reviewed literal as the optional `expectedMinReaderModel` tool argument. Definitions and instances carrying the facet require reader model 8. User assignees qualify through direct roles or the definition's role aliases, while collective role assignees must literally match one configured role. Studio assignment controls, including manual start, auto-start, and assignees nested in to-do rows, offer only eligible choices while retaining stale current values so editors can remove or replace them. Constrained pickers name the active eligible roles and distinguish an empty eligible set from a search with no matches. Top-level plural and composite edits retain no more occurrences of a stale assignment at each declared assignment location than the previous value contained; removal and reordering therefore work, while an added copy is a new assignment and must qualify. Direct singular replacements and every assignment present in an `updateWhere` fragment remain strict. Each engine verb uses one member-directory snapshot across retries, cascade hops, and spawned children, then the next verb reads current membership.

  Malformed project-member and project-user directory responses now fail loudly instead of treating bad rows or role records as missing users, and actor resolution reports those failures as `inaccessible`, so integrations can distinguish directory failures from absent membership.

  CLI `start` and `definition delete` no longer apply the definition-submission acknowledgement gate; deploy, check, dry-run, definition diff, Blueprint provision, and engine definition APIs still validate the selected definitions' required floor.

  No reader-fleet rollout or deployment-literal change is required for existing definitions that do not use `roles`.

  **Docs impact:** Update the assignment field reference and authoring examples for `roles`, distinguish eligibility from editability, action permission, and literal queue ownership, and add the model-8 conditional adoption sequence to the prerelease rollout guide.

- b0b1550: **BREAKING:** Product-prefixed telemetry events now use `Workflows <event>` instead of `Editorial Workflows <event>`; `EditorialWorkflowsResource` is replaced by `WorkflowsResource`; and `defineWorkflows` now generates `workflows-<deployment name>` resource names instead of `editorial-workflows-<deployment name>`. Telemetry consumers matching the previous literals stop receiving events until updated, TypeScript consumers importing the previous Blueprint interface no longer compile, and an existing Blueprint stack that relies on the generated name treats the new default as a different resource identity.

  Update telemetry dashboards, schemas, alerts, and queries to match the `Workflows` prefix; event suffixes, payloads, and versions are unchanged. Replace Blueprint imports with `WorkflowsResource`. Before deploying an existing Blueprint stack, either pass its recorded resource name explicitly or plan the detach-and-create migration to the new default. Workflows request-tag families and billing classification are unchanged.

  Other user-facing package copy now uses the Workflows product name. No upgrade action is required for consumers that do not match telemetry event names or use the Blueprint package.

  **Docs impact:** Rename the product throughout the public documentation, move the docs section to `/docs/workflows/*` with permanent redirects from every `/docs/editorial-workflows/*` path, and document the telemetry-prefix, `WorkflowsResource`, and Blueprint resource-name migrations in the telemetry reference, Blueprint guide, and release notes.

## 0.28.0

### Minor Changes

- 5050b06: **BREAKING:** Authoring a deployment now types through `WorkflowDeploymentInput` / `WorkflowConfigInput`, which require `expectedMinReaderModel` as the current reader-floor literal. Passing a parsed `WorkflowDeployment` / `WorkflowConfig` (where the floor is optional/unverified) into `defineWorkflowConfig` or `defineWorkflows` is a type error — share the authored deployment object instead of `config.deployments[n]`. The same pin shows up on the blueprint resource: `EditorialWorkflowsResource.deployment` and `parseWorkflowDeployment`'s return type are now `AcknowledgedDeployment` (floor asserted to the current literal), so a hand-constructed provider resource must carry that literal too.

  At runtime, config parse no longer rejects a stale or missing floor on an untargeted deployment. Only deployment-scoped commands assert, and only the selected deployment: definition deploy, `--check` / `--dry-run`, blueprint provision, `start`, `definition delete`, and `definition diff` (the last is a deployment-scoped read). Instance-id commands (`fire-action`, `abort`, `set-stage`, `reset-activity`) deliberately do not assert — they resolve by instance id, not by a declared deployment's acknowledgement — so an unacknowledged floor does not stop those instance commits.

  Upgrade TypeScript configs and blueprint manifests that fed a parsed deployment into those helpers: keep a shared authored object (`satisfies WorkflowDeploymentInput`) for both `defineWorkflowConfig` and `defineWorkflows`, and give any hand-built `EditorialWorkflowsResource` the current floor literal on `deployment`. Existing configs that already acknowledge the current floor keep working at runtime; a stale selected deployment still fails with `ReaderModelAcknowledgementError` (headline + short steps; the CLI renders it through the clean styled-error path).

  **Docs impact:** Update the CLI / blueprint authoring examples and the prerelease reader-floor guidance so they name `WorkflowConfigInput` / `WorkflowDeploymentInput` / `AcknowledgedDeployment`, forbid passing `config.deployments[n]` into `defineWorkflows`, state that instance-id writes are outside the acknowledgement gate, and stop implying whole-config parse-time rejection for commands that never select a deployment.

## 0.1.0

### Minor Changes

- 58f8211: New package: Sanity Blueprints integration for Editorial Workflows definition deploys. `defineWorkflows(deployment)` declares a deployment (the same shape as a `sanity.workflow.ts` `deployments[]` entry) as a `sanity.workflow` blueprint resource — validated eagerly at manifest evaluation (definition structure, GROQ, alias bindings, duplicate names, spawn cycles) and carried as pure data. `provisionWorkflowResource` is the provider core a blueprint resource provider runs: the engine's content-addressed, create-only definition deploy (create = update, idempotent, convergent). Definitions are retain-only through blueprints — the default lifecycle is `deletionPolicy: 'retain'`, a policy that promises deletion is rejected by the definer, and `destroyWorkflowResource` refuses unconditionally: deleting a definition stays a deliberate act through the workflow CLI's `definition delete`, never a side effect of a manifest edit.
